definition: Legendary prewar yokozuna who compiled an unbeaten 69-match winning streak — the longest in modern history.
Dominant yokozuna of the 1960s who won 32 career basho, a record that stood for more than two decades.
Popular yokozuna of the early 1970s known for his stylish sumo; became a beloved long-running TV commentator after retirement.
Powerful yokozuna of the mid-1970s who was renowned for his overwhelming strength and pushing attacks.
1970s yokozuna nicknamed 'Golden Left' for his decisive left-hand belt grip.
Became the youngest yokozuna in modern history at age 21 in 1974, going on to win 24 career basho.
Technically skilled yokozuna promoted in 1979, known for his lower-body strength and balance.
Known as 'The Wolf', this muscular yokozuna won 31 career basho in the 1980s and revived domestic interest in sumo.
Compact, fierce yokozuna of the late 1980s known for relentless pushing attacks.
Large, powerful yokozuna who competed in the same era as Chiyonofuji and Hokutoumi.
Born Chad Rowan in Hawaii, USA; became the first foreign-born yokozuna when promoted in 1993.
Immensely popular Japanese yokozuna of the 1990s who won 22 career basho and is considered one of the best ever.
Elder brother of Takanohana II and fellow yokozuna; their shared era in the mid-1990s drew record public interest.
Hawaiian-born yokozuna and the second foreigner to reach sumo's highest rank, winning 12 career basho.
The first Mongolian yokozuna, he dominated the early 2000s with an aggressive style and 25 career basho wins.
Widely regarded as the greatest rikishi of all time, with 45 career basho wins and 1,187 career victories.
Mongolian yokozuna renowned for his explosive speed and dynamic forward-charging sumo.
Mongolian yokozuna known for his technical belt sumo and calm, methodical approach.
The first Japanese-born yokozuna in 19 years when promoted in January 2017; deeply beloved by domestic fans.
Current yokozuna who overcame near-career-ending knee injuries to stage one of sumo's most remarkable comebacks.
